answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Franklin printed this himself in ‘Poor Richard Improved’ for 1756, on the April calendar page — one of hundreds of one-line proverbs in the almanac. The wording is confirmed verbatim in Ford’s 1889 scholarly collection of the almanacs ↗ and catalogued by the Yale Papers of Benjamin Franklin ↗.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt:
Be civil to all; sociable to many; familiar with few; Friend to one; enemy to none.
Vain-glory flowereth, but beareth no Fruit.
trail: The maxim appears verbatim under April in Ford’s 1889 collection of Franklin’s Poor Richard prefaces, proverbs & poems ↗, on the page headed “Poor Richard for 1756” — reading “sociable to many.”
The Yale Papers of Benjamin Franklin ↗ catalogue it in ‘Poor Richard Improved, 1756.’
The maxim is widely and correctly credited to Franklin on quote sites such as Goodreads ↗, matching the almanac wording.
source.cutTag: ↑ printed under April, immediately followed by “Vain-glory flowereth, but beareth no Fruit”
source.excerptNote: In the 1756 almanac the line sits on the April page, one of dozens of terse proverbs Franklin tucked between the calendar grid and the weather notes. The proverb that follows it — “Vain-glory flowereth, but beareth no Fruit” — is printed on the same page.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: About Benjamin Franklin
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was a printer, scientist, and Founding Father who published Poor Richard’s Almanack under the pen name “Richard Saunders” from 1733 to 1758. Its calendar pages carried hundreds of one-line proverbs that Franklin wrote, sharpened, or adapted from older collections. He freely admitted the sayings gathered “the Wisdom of many Ages and Nations,” which is why several — this one included — have the polished ring of an inherited maxim.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Poor Richard’s Almanack was Franklin’s bestseller and his soapbox: an annual almanac whose calendar pages he salted with pithy rules for living. Under the persona of the struggling astrologer “Richard Saunders,” Franklin sold tens of thousands of copies a year and, in the process, taught a young country its household philosophy of thrift, industry, and prudent sociability.

This little maxim is a graduated scale of intimacy — civility owed to everyone, sociability to many, closeness to a careful few, true friendship to one, and hostility to no one. It captures the cautious, networked temperament that Franklin practiced in business and diplomacy alike.
context.detailsSummary: On Franklin as compiler, not always originator
detailsBody: Franklin was candid that his proverbs were gleaned as much as invented. In the famous 1758 preface later called The Way to Wealth, he has Father Abraham quote “Poor Richard” while noting the sayings contained “the Wisdom of many Ages and Nations.” No specific pre-1756 source has been located for this particular line, but its balanced, aphoristic form is typical of the older conduct-book tradition Franklin drew on.
